name: Wei Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy rice, tea, noodles, sauces and dried goods for a family-run wholesaler that supplies about three hundred grocery shops and restaurants. I'm in by six, because the shopkeepers call early and want to be heard by a person. I walk the warehouse, check prices with the importers by phone, and write the orders by hand in a ledger before they go into the computer. Mr Lau, the owner, has known me for twenty-six years. What tires me is that younger staff want to change everything, and the margins are thinner each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, good, let the machines do their little tasks and leave the buying to people who know the shops. At home I'd tell Mei not to worry. Online I'd say nothing, I don't talk about work with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still feel uneasy. The margins are thin, the big supermarkets undercut us, and Mr Lau is nearly seventy with no one to take over. If the firm is sold, the new owners will cut the older, higher-paid staff, and I am one. That has nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as always, keep my ledger and phone calls, and save what I can, maybe a little more each month. I'd keep going to church and the community. I'd also quietly ask Mr Lau about his plans, since a loyal man should know where he stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. It's not fear, it's a feeling that the ground is shifting under the whole trade, not only me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on. What still worries you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next owners. Mr Lau's son lives abroad and isn't interested. If an investment company buys us, they will say efficiency and then count heads. I've seen it at other wholesalers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to at work about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Lau himself, and my old colleague Tan, who works with me on the tea. We've talked for years. We'd say the same thing, that we're only as safe as the owner is healthy.

say: At work I'd say let the machines do **little tasks** and leave the buying to people who know the shops.
At home I'd tell Mei not to worry.
think: I still feel uneasy: **thin margins** and a nearly seventy owner with no successor.
If the firm is sold, new owners may cut **older, higher-paid** staff like me.
do: Keep my **ledger** and phone calls as always.
Quietly ask Mr Lau about his **plans**.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a sense the whole trade's ground is shifting.
S0.quote: If an investment company buys us, they will say efficiency and then count heads.
fieldNote: His fear is **about ownership, not technology**, and he reads the future through what happened at other wholesalers.
He speaks of **loyalty and trust**, and wants to know where he stands with the owner.

steps.text: Keep the ledger and daily supplier phone calls going
Save a little more each month
Ask Mr Lau directly about his plans for the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful. At work I'd say a machine can't taste tea or know which shopkeeper is behind on his bills. At home I'd say it's the young people's world now, and we should help them without being pushed aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried. Ordering and checking prices are thinking work, and a computer could do them. I'm slow with new systems and I know it. If the firm hires two young people with software, I'd be the expensive one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself necessary where the computer can't reach: the shopkeepers, the importers, the tea itself. I'd learn the minimum I'm told to, grudgingly. I'd save more, perhaps 250 a month, and I'd talk to Mei about when I'd stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still think I have some say, but I don't like how fast it's moving. I'd feel old, and that's an ugly feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekly reorders. Rice, noodles, soy sauce, the same every week for twenty years. A computer would do that in seconds. Prices with the importers, no. They won't speak to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm told you to use the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'm asked, politely, because I won't be the man who refused. But I'd also check its work by hand at first. When it's wrong, I'd say so openly. It's honest, not stubborn.

say: At work I'd say a machine **can't taste tea** or know which shopkeeper is behind on bills.
At home I'd say we should help the young without being **pushed aside**.
think: Ordering and price checks are **thinking work** a computer could do.
If the firm hires two young people with software, I'd be the **expensive one**.
do: Make myself **necessary** with shopkeepers, importers and the tea.
Learn only the **minimum** I'm told to, grudgingly.
Save **250 a month** and talk with Mei about when to stop.
feel: **Anxious**, feeling old and watching things move fast.
S1.quote: Rice, noodles, soy sauce, the same every week for twenty years. A computer would do that in seconds.
fieldNote: He is **loyal and proud**, and sees his value in tea knowledge and importer relationships.
He admits he is **slow with new systems**, and that admission is the root of his anxiety.

steps.text: Deepen ties with shopkeepers and importers the software can't reach
Talk with Mei about when I would stop work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster and it was never voted on by anybody. At work I'd say we need honest warning. At church I'd say, pray, but also prepare. Online, I'd say the big technology firms should answer for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm finished by 2028. All my work is thinking work and a machine does it. The robots three years later would clear the warehouse too. There'd be no job left for a man who's slow to change, at 58 with two months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd go through every expense with Mei and cut it to the bone. I'd ask Mr Lau for a conversation about my pension and a fair exit. I'd sell the second car. I'd also ask my son-in-law, who has a trade business, whether there's any work I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep, and I'd be short with Mei. I'd feel ashamed, as if it were my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mr Lau, you've been fair to me for twenty-six years. Tell me honestly what's coming. If you must let me go, let me go with my pension intact and a fair payment. I'd not beg, but I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you speak to Mr Lau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei says we have each other and the church. That's worth a lot. But I'd hate to depend on the congregation's charity. I'd want to earn.

say: I'd say this is **a disaster** that nobody ever voted on.
I'd say the big technology firms should **answer** for it.
think: I think I'm **finished by 2028**, and robots later clear the warehouse too.
There'd be no job for a man **slow to change**, with two months saved.
do: Go through every expense with Mei and **cut to the bone**.
Ask Mr Lau for a **fair exit** and my pension.
feel: **Alarmed**, ashamed, as if it were my fault.
S2.quote: Mr Lau, you've been fair to me for twenty-six years. Tell me honestly what's coming.
fieldNote: He is **alarmed and ashamed**, a man whose self-worth is bound to his work.
He plans to **ask** his owner for honesty, not beg, and dislikes the idea of congregation charity.

steps.text: Go through every expense with Mei and cut to the bone
Ask Mr Lau for a fair exit and my full pension
Ask my son-in-law about work in his trade business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a little time to prepare and we must use it. I'd say it to Mr Lau and to the congregation. I'd say apprenticeships and work are better than any handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's still frightening. I'd be 63 and my skills would be worth less every year. I'd have time to fix money, not to become a new person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to save hard, clear the mortgage, and ask Mr Lau for a plan for the old staff. I'd teach the young buyers everything I know about tea and rice, so that the shops get what they need. And I'd put a date on my retirement, say 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slowly. Five years is not a punch, it's a rising tide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. Does it feel better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little better, yes. It lets me fix what I can. But I won't pretend that makes me comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be useful to the end. The teaching would help me feel that. I'd hate to just sit and wait.

say: I'd say five years is a **little time** and must be used.
I'd say **apprenticeships** and work beat any handout.
think: It's still frightening: at 63 my skills would be **worth less** every year.
The time lets me fix **money**, not become a new person.
do: Ask Mr Lau for a **plan** for the old staff.
Teach the young buyers **tea and rice** knowledge.
feel: **Alarmed** but slowly, like a rising tide.
S3.quote: Five years is not a punch, it's a rising tide.
fieldNote: He wants **useful** to the end, and uses the extra years for mentoring the young buyers.
His **work as dignity** shapes how he judges handouts and apprenticeships.

steps.text: Save hard and clear the mortgage within five years
Ask Mr Lau for a plan for the older staff
Teach the young buyers tea and rice knowledge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair length of time. I'd say the schools and workplaces should prepare the young with real trades and apprenticeships. And I'd say the family must stay together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 and retired. So it isn't my own work I fear for. I'd fear for my grandchildren, and for the shops and the little firms like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62 or 63 and retire. I'd mentor the young buyers, keep up with my church work, and live modestly. I'd also help my son-in-law with his small business if he needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for others, not for me. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Does it feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a trade or a skill that needs hands and presence, to save, and to keep faith and family close. Don't depend on one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprenticeships especially. People who can fix things and serve people will always be needed. I'd say that to any young person.

say: I'd say schools and workplaces should prepare the young with **real trades** and apprenticeships.
I'd say the **family** must stay together.
think: I'd be **retired** by then, so I fear for my grandchildren and small firms like ours.
Ten years is long enough that **I'd probably get through**.
do: Mentor the young **buyers** and keep up church work.
S4.quote: People who can fix things and serve people will always be needed.
fieldNote: With ten years his fear is **for the next generation** and small family firms, not himself.
He turns to **trades and apprenticeships**, in line with his traditional outlook.

steps.text: Mentor the young buyers before I leave
Help my son-in-law's small business if he needs me

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm 58, and I have about two months of savings, which is not much. My wife Mei still works part-time at our church's office, and our children are grown but not rich. I'd want honest notice, my full pension, and a chance to work as long as I can, not a handout. I'd also ask Mr Lau to keep his word to the old staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of hard work. I'm afraid of being made useless by something nobody asked for. People who've given their lives to a trade deserve some respect, and I don't see much of it.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of hard work. I'm afraid of being made useless by something nobody asked for.
portrait: **Wei** is 58, a senior buyer of rice, tea and dried goods for a family-run wholesaler serving local grocery shops.
He is **traditional and resistant**, never uses AI tools, and writes orders in a ledger before they go on the computer.
He favours free markets, work and community, **dislikes handouts**, and blames big technology firms and distant investors.
With about **two months saved** and a wife working part-time, his cushion is the thinnest of any in his family circle.
His worry rises steadily as the clock shortens, and he wants **honest notice** and his pension more than retraining.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because he'd be made useless with little savings and a pension still ahead.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **honest notice**, his full pension and the chance to work as long as he can, not a handout.
